heard: You miss the ox by 37 pounds, the crowd by nine. The crowd aren't experts. Most of them are guessing two. Plymouth 1906. 787 people pay six cents each to guess an ox's weight. Collect every ticket and sort them, lightest to heaviest. Take the one in the middle. The wild guesses at the ends can't move it. 1 ,207 pounds. The ox weighed 1 ,198. Off by nine. But half the tickets missed by more than 37. So why is the middle so close? Each guess is the weight plus a mistake. Too high or too low about as often. In the middle they cancel. Your mistake stands alone. The crowds cancel out. Francis Galton sorted every ticket to check. Five friends guessed 10, 12, 30, 14, and 11 suites. What's the crowd's guess?
